title: What a Fresh 48-Month Inspection Really Means
hook: It comes due whether the aircraft flew 400 hours or 40.
body:
Some of the biggest inspections on business jets aren't triggered by hours flown — they're triggered by the calendar. The 48-month is one of those. It's scheduled, it's expensive, and time keeps moving toward it no matter how the aircraft was operated.

That means real downtime at a shop, on top of whatever the invoice runs. When you see a listing with a fresh 48-month, the buyer is inheriting a clean slate instead of that bill — typically around four years before it comes due again.

Here's the part that trips people up: the asking price is only part of the true cost. Where an aircraft sits in its inspection cycle is the other part. Two aircraft priced almost identically can be worlds apart once you factor in what's coming due.

Before you compare listings side by side, ask where each one sits in its maintenance cycle. It's one of the first things we look at for every client, buyer or seller.
cta: Talk to Vertical Jet Sales before you compare listings — we'll tell you what's actually due.
